name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,376

clue.text: Fit for boxing match

blocks.note: the noun: a sudden attack or spell, as of coughing

explanation.surface: A boxer is declared in good enough shape for the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' reads as the adjective 'healthy'; here it is the noun, a sudden spell of something, as in a bout of coughing.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one noun: a spell of illness, and a single contest in the ring.

clue.text: Reaction when Charlie comes right up in striking garment

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' is towards the top, and 'right up' takes the C all the way to first place

blocks.note: the starting word, whose fourth letter is a C
Charlie = C in the NATO alphabet: the letter that moves

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie turns up in an eye-catching outfit and gets a reaction.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves, so this is a rearrangement of the gentlest kind. 'Charlie' looks like a person arriving at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Fashion usage: a designer's showpiece outfit is called by this name.

clue.text: False hair singular on hag

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'on' means placed above

blocks.note: a hag is an ugly old woman or witch

explanation.surface: An old hag wears a single hairpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: A switch is a hank of false hair worn to add length or bulk, a sense many solvers do not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A less familiar sense: a detached tress of hair added to one's own.

clue.text: Manage to hear end of story, easy to remember

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: to catch what someone says is to manage to hear it

explanation.surface: A listener strains to catch the end of a memorable story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of story' sounds like a conversation closer; it is simply the letter Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Said of tunes and slogans that stick in the head after one hearing.

clue.text: Minimum of check fabric in drawer

indicators.note: the smallest possible part of 'check' is a single letter, its first

explanation.surface: A small checked cloth lies folded in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' looks like furniture; it is something that draws.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful sense: a drawer is anything that draws, and a wax stick used for colouring is one.

clue.text: Orderly is fairly big

blocks.note: the adjective: neat, in good order
informal: considerable, as of a sum of money

explanation.surface: A hospital orderly is described as quite a large man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly' looks like a hospital attendant; it is the adjective 'neat'. A tidy sum is a sizeable one.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one adjective: neat, and (informally) sizeable.

clue.text: From shelf you moved domestic pest

indicators.note: letters that have been moved no longer stand in their original places

explanation.surface: Someone is told they shifted a household pest off a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal: a fly sitting on a shelf is exactly the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the common fly that lives around homes is a nuisance insect.

clue.text: Horror regularly in recess for library user

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter
the extracted letters are placed within the recess

blocks.note: hOrRoR: second, fourth and sixth letters
a bower is a shady nook or retreat in a garden

explanation.surface: Something frightening lurks in an alcove of the library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horror' looks like the thing lurking; only its even letters are used, and they go in after the first letter of the recess.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain description: someone who takes books out of a library on loan.

clue.text: A right grim passion

explanation.surface: Someone's strong feeling is described as grimly intense.
explanation.walkthrough: Note the British spelling with -OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both mean intense, fervent feeling.

clue.text: That sly European suspect is trying to escape notice

indicators.note: as an adjective, 'suspect' means unreliable, so the letters cannot be trusted in their order

explanation.surface: A shifty foreign suspect is lying low to avoid being spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as a noun, a person under suspicion; it is the adjective telling you the letters are unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: moving quietly and secretly so as not to be seen.

clue.text: One marsh turns into desert

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the other way, so the letters read backwards

explanation.surface: A swamp dries up and becomes a desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns into' reads as 'becomes', but only 'turns' is wordplay; 'into' just joins the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the great desert of Mongolia and northern China.

clue.text: Unexpurgated novel

blocks.note: with nothing cut out, as first written

explanation.surface: A book is published uncensored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, which suits 'unexpurgated'; it is the adjective 'new'.
explanation.definitionFit: One adjective covers both: the uncut first version, and something new and inventive.

clue.text: Pushes away — don't touch!

blocks.note: a rugby move: fending off a tackler with an open palm
a common exclamation warning someone away

explanation.surface: Someone shoves another person away and snaps at them not to touch.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is the verb 'hand off' in the third person, a rugby move; the second is the exclamation 'Hands off!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb in the third person, and the same words as a warning cry.

clue.text: Expert participant in tea ceremony

indicators.note: a participant is part of something, so the answer is part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A skilled guest takes part in a formal Japanese tea ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between 'tea' and 'ceremony'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: someone outstandingly skilled.

clue.text: Expressing disappointment about time for rare viewing

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher sighs over the long wait for a glimpse of a rare bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' reads as part of 'time for', but it is the link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a brief glimpse of something seldom seen, as of a rare bird or a UFO.

clue.text: Secure small whisky, for example, in provincial capital

blocks.note: to secure a prize is to win it
a nip is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: Someone gets hold of a small whisky in a Canadian city.
explanation.walkthrough: A fitting answer for a Canadian paper: the definition is Canadian, where 'province' is the unit of government.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital city of Manitoba.

clue.text: Eclair for one finished extremely readily

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone polished off an eclair very eagerly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely readily' reads as 'very eagerly'; it means only the end letters of 'readily'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'for one': an eclair is one kind of baked sweet.

clue.text: Gaudy decoration, not new

explanation.surface: Some flashy ornament is described as old rather than new.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'not new' look like a comment on the decoration; it is the instruction to drop a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both mean showy and tasteless.

clue.text: Men’s appearance to the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so what counts is the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: a guise is an outward appearance

explanation.surface: How a group of men present themselves to the people watching.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S is 'is', joining 'Men' to the wordplay rather than making it possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym for men or fellows.

clue.text: Clothes that may be changed in car

definitions.text: that may be changed in car

blocks.clueFragment: that may be changed in car
blocks.note: a driver shifts between these to change speed

explanation.surface: Someone changes clothes in the back of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a hurried change of outfit; the second meaning is the gearbox.
explanation.definitionFit: Two nouns: informal for outfit or kit, and a toothed ratio in a gearbox.

clue.text: Plan gets a try, disastrously

indicators.note: something that goes disastrously falls apart, so the letters end up in disarray

explanation.surface: A scheme is attempted and goes badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets' is fodder, not a link word; every letter of 'gets a try' is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a scheme for reaching a goal.

clue.text: Barrier that often puts end to scandal

blocks.note: a hinged barrier across a path or fence
the suffix journalists attach to a scandal's name, after the Watergate affair

explanation.surface: A barrier that keeps gossip out.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is the suffix from Watergate, as in 'Partygate'; 'puts end to' means sits at the end of, not stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun for a barrier, and the stock suffix of scandal names.

clue.text: Meaning of “camping”?

blocks.note: the surface asks for a dictionary definition of a word
read instead as a description of where a camper sleeps, in two words

explanation.surface: A request for the definition of the word 'camping'.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer IN TENT and it describes someone camping; read whole, it is a synonym of 'Meaning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: purpose or meaning, as in the intent of a remark.

clue.text: No teaser managed to receive sympathetic response

indicators.note: letters that are managed are handled and arranged, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: A plain-speaking puzzle, with no tricks, wins over its audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Managed' reads as 'succeeded'; it tells you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: an idea that strikes a chord meets with agreement.

clue.text: Left inside like a cat in light snowfall

indicators.note: 'inside' places the first element within the next

explanation.surface: A cat stays indoors while light snow falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left inside' pictures the cat kept indoors; it is L placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a brief, gusty fall of snow.
